title: Ordering Food in Spanish: Restaurant Phrases That Work

body_html:
Ordering food in Spanish is often the first real conversation travelers and learners have, and it’s a great confidence builder. Restaurant language is predictable: you ask for a table, look at the menu, order, maybe ask a question or two, and pay. But there are regional habits that surprise learners, like waiters who never bring the check until you ask, or bars where you order tapas at the counter. Here’s everything you need.

Key takeaways
  • Order with Para mí…, Quería… or ¿Me da…?
  • Ask for recommendations: ¿Qué me recomienda?
  • Ask for the check: La cuenta, por favor. It won’t come until you do.
  • Many places offer a set lunch menu: el menú del día.
{{toc}}

Arriving and getting a table

  • Buenas noches. Una mesa para dos, por favor. Good evening. A table for two, please.
  • Tengo una reserva a nombre de Clark. I have a reservation under Clark.
  • ¿Podemos sentarnos en la terraza? Can we sit on the terrace?
  • ¿Hay que esperar mucho? Is there a long wait?

Ordering food in Spanish: menus and recommendations

  • ¿Me trae la carta, por favor? Could you bring me the menu?
  • ¿Tienen menú del día? Do you have a set menu of the day?
  • ¿Qué me recomienda? What do you recommend?
  • ¿Cuál es la especialidad de la casa? What’s the house speciality?
  • ¿Qué lleva este plato? What’s in this dish?

In Spain, la carta is the full menu and el menú is a fixed-price set menu. In much of Latin America, el menú is the menu itself. The RAE dictionary lists both meanings.

Placing your order

SpanishEnglish
Para mí, la sopa de primero.For me, the soup as an appetizer.
Quería el pollo, por favor.I’d like the chicken, please.
¿Me pone una caña?Could I have a small beer? (Spain)
¿Me da unos tacos al pastor?Could I have some tacos al pastor? (Mexico)
De segundo, el pescado.For the main course, the fish.
Lo mismo para mí.The same for me.

For steak: poco hecho (rare), al punto (medium), muy hecho (well done). For politeness tips, see {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Drinks

  • Agua sin gas / con gas. Still / sparkling water.
  • ¿Agua del grifo? Tap water? (in Spain, usually free if you ask)
  • Una copa de vino tinto / blanco. A glass of red / white wine.
  • Un café con leche / un cortado. A white coffee / a coffee with a dash of milk.

Dietary needs and allergies

  • Soy vegetariano/a. ¿Qué platos no llevan carne? I’m vegetarian. Which dishes have no meat?
  • Soy alérgico/a a los frutos secos. I’m allergic to nuts.
  • ¿Esto lleva gluten? Does this contain gluten?
  • Sin cebolla, por favor. Without onion, please.
  • ¿Pica mucho? Is it very spicy?

Careful: in Spain, a dish described as vegetarian might still include tuna or ham; ask specifically: ¿Lleva atún o jamón?

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

During the meal

  • ¿Nos trae más pan, por favor? Could you bring us more bread?
  • Perdone, esto está frío. Excuse me, this is cold.
  • Todo está buenísimo. Everything is delicious. (see {{link:how-to-compliment-food-in-spanish|how to compliment food in Spanish}})
  • ¿Qué tienen de postre? What do you have for dessert?

Paying and tipping

  • La cuenta, por favor. The check, please.
  • ¿Me cobra, por favor? Can I pay, please? (Spain)
  • ¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta? Can I pay by card?
  • ¿Pagamos por separado? Shall we pay separately?
  • Invito yo. It’s on me.

Tipping varies. In Spain, tips are modest and optional; rounding up or leaving a few euros is common. In Mexico, around 10–15% is customary. In Argentina, around 10% is standard. When in doubt, ask a local: ¿Aquí se suele dejar propina?

Cultural notes

Meal times are later than in the US, especially in Spain, where lunch is often around 2 p.m. and dinner after 9 p.m. Waiters won’t rush you or bring the check uninvited; lingering is part of the experience, and the sobremesa after a meal can last hours. In tapas bars, you often order at the counter and pay at the end. Getting a waiter’s attention with ¡Perdone! or eye contact is fine; clicking your fingers is not. More etiquette in {{link:spanish-politeness-mistakes|Spanish politeness mistakes}}.

A sample conversation

  • Waiter: Buenas noches. ¿Qué van a tomar? (Good evening. What would you like?)
  • You: Para mí, el gazpacho de primero y la dorada de segundo. (For me, the gazpacho as an appetizer and the sea bream as a main.)
  • Waiter: Muy bien. ¿Y para beber? (Very good. And to drink?)
  • You: Una botella de agua sin gas y una copa de vino blanco, por favor. (A bottle of still water and a glass of white wine, please.)
  • Later: ¿Nos trae la cuenta cuando pueda? (Could you bring us the check when you can?)

Notice the structure most menus follow in Spain: primero (first course), segundo (main) and postre (dessert). The menú del día, served at lunchtime on weekdays, usually includes all three plus bread and a drink for a fixed price, and it is one of the best-value ways to eat well.

Common mistakes

MistakeBetterWhy
Quiero un café. (can sound blunt)¿Me da un café? / Un café, por favor.Softer request
Puedo tener la cuenta?¿Me trae la cuenta?Literal translation
Estoy completo.Estoy lleno.Completo is wrong here
Quiero un pez.Quiero pescado.Pez = live fish

Final thoughts

Greet, ask for the menu, order with para mí or ¿me da?, mention any allergies, and ask for the check when you’re ready. Enjoy the slow pace; in Spanish-speaking countries, a meal is an event. For more everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you order food in Spanish?
faq.a: Use Para mí…, Quería… or ¿Me da…?, followed by por favor. In Spain you’ll also hear ¿Me pone…?

faq.q: How do you ask for the check in Spanish?
faq.a: La cuenta, por favor (in Spain, also ¿Me cobra, por favor?). Waiters usually don’t bring it until you ask.

faq.q: How do you say you have an allergy in Spanish?
faq.a: Soy alérgico/a a… (I’m allergic to…), for example Soy alérgica a los frutos secos.
